action_criteria.expected_evidence: Expansile infiltrative T2/FLAIR-hyperintense left frontoparietal mass (4.1 cm) with two faint enhancing foci up to 8 mm, no necrosis or restricted diffusion, corona radiata and callosal extension and 2 mm midline shift
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium (tumour protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to characterise the left frontoparietal lesion, define mass effect and plan surgery
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion and FLAIR is the standard imaging for a suspected diffuse glioma: it defines the enhancing target, the oedema and the mass effect, and plans the surgical approach (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: rCBV 2.6 at the posterior enhancing foci and intermediate in the core, identifying the sampling target
action_criteria.label: Order MR perfusion (DSC) to assess tumour vascularity and target the most aggressive region for tissue sampling
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated rCBV supports a high-grade neoplasm and identifies the region to sample; it does not grade or exclude, tissue decides (Law 2003).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Cho/NAA 3.4 at the enhancing focus with only trace lipid and no lactate; Cho/NAA 1.9 in the core
action_criteria.label: Order MR spectroscopy (1H-MRS) to characterise the metabolic profile of the lesion
action_criteria.rationale: Elevated choline with reduced NAA and lipid-lactate supports a high-grade neoplasm; it does not establish the diagnosis, tissue does (Bulik 2013).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No contraindication to surgery: normal counts, electrolytes and coagulation; type and screen done
action_criteria.label: Order pre-operative laboratory work-up: CBC, metabolic panel, coagulation (PT/INR, aPTT) and type and screen before neurosurgery
action_criteria.rationale: A neurosurgical procedure and corticosteroids are anticipated; platelets, coagulation, electrolytes and glucose must be known before either.

action_criteria.rationale: The choice between standard and hypofractionated treatment after the integrated diagnosis turns on age and KPS, with KPS under 70 the unfavourable threshold (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.label: Order functional MRI to map premotor, supplementary motor and primary motor cortex relative to the lesion before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The lesion lies close to premotor cortex and the hand motor area; functional mapping plans a maximal safe resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left corticospinal tract through the FLAIR abnormality, about 3 mm from the enhancing focus
action_criteria.label: Order DTI tractography of the corticospinal tract in the corona radiata before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The lesion and its oedema lie close to the left corticospinal tract in the corona radiata; tractography plans a maximal safe resection (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, CNS WHO grade 3 with IDH1 R132H mutation, ATRX loss, 1p/19q intact, no CDKN2A/B homozygous deletion, no necrosis or microvascular proliferation, and MGMT promoter methylated
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the left frontoparietal lesion, or stereotactic biopsy of the enhancing foci if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, IDH1/IDH2 sequencing, ATRX immunohistochemistry, 1p/19q codeletion, CDKN2A/B deletion and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment. In an IDH-mutant astrocytoma, homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion assigns grade 4 even without necrosis or microvascular proliferation, so grade 3 cannot be called without it (WHO 2021; EANO 2021).

action_criteria.label: Check drug interactions for dexamethasone against the current medicines
action_criteria.rationale: Dexamethasone will be started; the current medicines and allergy are checked before prescribing.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform a lumbar puncture: the left frontoparietal mass causes midline shift and ventricular compression, and the pressure gradient risks herniation.
Do not attribute the changed, refractory headaches to the prior migraine: a new headache pattern with cognitive change and a mass lesion is structural.
Do not start radiotherapy or chemotherapy before the integrated tissue diagnosis: treatment differs between grades 2, 3 and 4.
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the left frontoparietal lesion, with preoperative functional MRI and DTI tractography and intraoperative mapping, with stereotactic biopsy of the enhancing, highest-rCBV foci if resection is not safely feasible; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5) including IDH, ATRX, 1p/19q, CDKN2A/B and MGMT.

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic oedema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for astrocytoma, IDH-mutant, CNS WHO grade 3 the standard is radiotherapy followed by adjuvant temozolomide (EANO 2021), here at age 45 with KPS 80 and a methylated MGMT promoter.

clinical_pearls: Not all high-grade gliomas are ring-enhancing with central necrosis: an IDH-mutant astrocytoma of CNS WHO grade 3 often presents as a predominantly non-enhancing infiltrative mass; perfusion and spectroscopy identify the most aggressive region to sample, and tissue assigns the grade
rCBV >1.75 on DSC perfusion MRI is the validated threshold for distinguishing high-grade from low-grade glioma; an rCBV of 2.6 in a predominantly non-enhancing lesion should trigger high-grade workup

WHO 2021 grades IDH-mutant astrocytoma on histology and CDKN2A/B: elevated mitotic activity without necrosis, microvascular proliferation or homozygous CDKN2A/B deletion is grade 3; the deletion alone makes it grade 4

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Arjun Mehta is a 45-year-old right-handed software architect with a well-documented history of migraine without aura, in remission for the past three years on propranolol prophylaxis. He presents to the neurology inpatient service after an outpatient CT, ordered by his primary care physician, showed a left frontoparietal abnormality. He first noticed a change in his headaches approximately six weeks ago: attacks became more frequent (daily to near-daily), the quality shifted from his typical unilateral throbbing migraines to a diffuse dull pressure that is worst upon awakening and persists through the morning, and his usual sumatriptan rescue provided only partial and transient relief. He initially dismissed the change as stress-related, since he had recently taken on a demanding new project at work, and consulted his primary care physician, who increased the propranolol dose with no improvement. Three weeks ago, his wife noticed he was making uncharacteristic errors in everyday tasks: forgetting grocery items, losing his train of thought mid-sentence during dinner conversations, and failing to complete a weekly family financial review that he had managed without difficulty for years. On direct questioning, Mr. Mehta acknowledges mild word-finding pauses during high-pressure conversations but attributes them to fatigue. He denies any visual changes, limb weakness, or sensory symptoms. He has had no seizures and no episodes of loss of consciousness. He has lost approximately 3 kg over the past six weeks without intentional dietary change, which he attributes to reduced appetite. He denies nausea, vomiting, or fever. His propranolol and sumatriptan doses were adjusted twice over the past month without benefit. Given the refractory and qualitatively altered headache pattern plus the emerging cognitive changes, his primary care physician ordered a non-contrast CT of the head, which showed an ill-defined left frontoparietal hypodensity with mild local mass effect, and recommended inpatient evaluation. He was admitted to the neurology service for urgent workup.
